A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question a, wording: The right option is the only one about something increasing ('More'), while the other three all say 'Less' or 'Fewer'. A student could pick the odd one out without knowing the idea, and the clue ('more of what is used and thrown away') points straight to it.

rejected.title: Environmental effects of cities
card: As a city grows, it uses more water and energy. It also makes more waste and more emissions, such as gases from cars and power stations.
Building on more land can remove bushland and farmland. Hard surfaces such as roads and roofs change how rainwater runs off.
Dense cities fit more people on less land. People living close together can share services like public transport, water pipes and power lines more efficiently.
So a growing city can add pressure on the environment, and how it is planned can reduce that pressure.
rejected.remember: Growing cities use more resources and make more waste, but density can share services well.

a.q: Which is a likely environmental effect of a growing city?
opts: More waste and emissions are produced
Less water and energy are used
Less land is built on
Fewer vehicles are on the roads
a.why: More people means more waste and emissions. Water and energy use usually rises, not falls, as a city grows.
a.clue: More people means more of what is used and thrown away.

b.q: Two cities have the same number of people. Riverton has apartments near train lines. Hillvale has houses spread over a wide area. What is a likely environmental advantage of Riverton?
opts: Shared services like trains reach more people per kilometre
It covers more land, so more farmland stays in use
Its homes have big yards, so more rainwater soaks in
It has fewer people, so it uses less water and energy
b.why: In a dense city, people live close together, so trains, pipes and power lines can serve many people over a short distance. Riverton has the same number of people as Hillvale, so it cannot use less because it is smaller. Big yards and more land describe spread-out Hillvale, not Riverton.
b.clue: Check which city each option really describes.

card: As a city grows, it uses more water and energy. It also makes more waste and more emissions, such as gases from cars and power stations.

Dense cities can also have benefits. Many people living close together can share services like public transport, water pipes and power lines more efficiently.

draft.remember: Growing cities use more resources and make more waste, but density can share services well.

a.q: Which is a likely environmental effect of a growing city?
opts: More waste and emissions are produced
Less water and energy are used
Less land is built on
Fewer vehicles are on the roads
a.why: More people means more waste and emissions. Water and energy use usually rises, not falls, as a city grows.
a.clue: More people means more of what is used and thrown away.

b.q: A planner says that a dense city can be better for the environment than a spread-out one. Which reason fits the card?
opts: Services like public transport can be shared by more people
Dense cities make no waste or emissions
Dense cities use no water or energy
Dense cities have more bushland inside them
b.why: With people living close together, services such as public transport and pipes can serve more people at once. Dense cities still use resources and make waste, so the other options are wrong.
b.clue: Think about who can share a train line.

a.best: More waste and emissions are produced

b.best: Services like public transport can be shared by more people
